title.text: EDSA Shrine (Mary, Queen of Peace Shrine)

title_en.text: EDSA Shrine (Mary, Queen of Peace Shrine)

tagline.text: A bronze Marian shrine at the gateway to Ortigas, honoring People Power

location.label: Location
location.text: Ugong Norte, Quezon City, at the corner of EDSA and Ortigas Avenue

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~500 (per person, city transport and a light meal)

children.text: The EDSA Shrine is a Marian shrine built by the Archdiocese of Manila in thanksgiving for the 1986 People Power Revolution, at the corner where EDSA meets Ortigas Avenue. A 10.7 m bronze statue of Mary, an underground church and reliefs of the revolutions make it a place of prayer and memory in the middle of the city.

The shrine's official name is the Shrine of Mary, Queen of Peace, and locally it is simply called the EDSA Shrine or Our Lady of EDSA. According to Wikipedia, it stands in Barangay Ugong Norte, Quezon City, at the corner of EDSA (Circumferential Road 4) and Ortigas Avenue, right next to Robinsons Galleria at the northern tip of Ortigas Center. It belongs to the Archdiocese of Manila, and its location makes it an easy stop during shopping or business in Ortigas.
The shrine began with the
1986 People Power Revolution

. Two days after the Marcos family went into exile, Cardinal Jaime Sin, the Archbishop of Manila, reportedly proposed building a shrine as a thanksgiving to the Virgin Mary. The first plan was to build it inside Camp Crame, but that was dropped because a church on state-owned land would have had to be ecumenical, so the corner lot donated by the Ortigas and Gokongwei families was chosen. The Filipino architect Francisco Mañosa designed it; it was inaugurated on December 8, 1989, the Feast of the Immaculate Conception, and dedicated to Mary on the 15th of the same month.

The shrine returned to the center of history during the Second EDSA Revolution in 2001. After President Estrada was deposed, Cardinal Sin declared it holy ground, and a marker recording this was later installed. Many other rallies and Masses have been held here, so for Filipinos it is both a religious site and a kind of civic square. Wikipedia notes that the National Commission for Culture and the Arts declared it an Important Cultural Property in 2019, and that the CBCP made it a National Shrine on January 25, 2025.

It is not a place with a long list of sights. Still, strolling past the bronze statue, the plaza, the reliefs and the underground church makes a meaningful 30 minutes to 1 hour and helps you understand modern Philippine history. Because it is a place of worship, modest dress and a quiet manner are the basics. Remember that it is a working church where Mass is held every day, not just an attraction, and it becomes clear where to take photos and where to pause. You may also see office workers around Ortigas drop in on their lunch break to pray.

blocks.title: The bronze statue of Our Lady of EDSA

children.text: Sculpted by Virginia Ty-Navarro in 1989, the bronze statue is about

long (some sources say 35 ft) and is reported to weigh about 8 tonnes, a figure recorded only in Wikipedia. Mary wears a crown and golden robes, with outstretched arms and an exposed Immaculate Heart, and white doves at her hands and feet. A popular story says it was carried in by helicopter because the roads were too narrow.

This is the promenade plaza spreading out around the statue. Mañosa imagined a "People's Basilica," a bahay kubo, the traditional Filipino house, scaled up, and this plaza is its open space. It is a good place for photos, but people are praying here, so keep your voice down. Many visitors take selfies below the statue; shifting your angle a little keeps other people's prayers from filling your frame and is easier on everyone.

The lower podium carries reliefs of the First People Power Revolution in 1986 and the Second in 2001. Seeing both revolutions in one place gives even visitors who know little about the events a sense of the mood. Check the details of the scenes in person.

The sanctuary is an underground church inspired by the Cathedral of Brasília. The organ is on the right side, and when no Mass is going on you can pray quietly. During Mass, be careful about entering and taking photos.

Francisco Mañosa is an architect known for designs that use indigenous materials and suit the tropical climate. His original concept was seven pitched roofs clustered around the statue, but the building as constructed took the form of a plaza and an underground church.
An adoration chapel is reported on the EDSA side. On Sundays there are several Masses from morning to evening, so even non-Catholics can watch local religious life up close.

Masses and events mark the revolution around February 25 each year. Wikipedia records a Mass for the 38th anniversary in 2024, and the shrine's official site announced events for the 40th anniversary (2026). Expect more crowds and security checks than usual, so allow extra time. The program changes every year, so check the official site's announcements first.

items.title: One-hour route
items.subtitle: A look at the statue and the church

children.text: Start on the EDSA side with a view of the statue from the front, and look for the doves at the bronze figure's hands and feet.
Walk around People's Plaza and look at the podium reliefs. Compare the 1986 and 2001 scenes in order.
If no Mass is under way, step quietly into the underground church and sit for a while.
Leave by the Ortigas Avenue side and have lunch or coffee at Robinsons Galleria next door.
Mass times can change, so check the shrine's official website or Facebook page before you go.
Look around the shrine and, if it is a Sunday, try attending the 9 o'clock Mass.
Have an early lunch at Robinsons Galleria.
Browse the shopping streets around
SM Megamall
or
Ortigas Center
Take the train at MRT-3 Ortigas Station before the evening rush begins.
From any MRT-3 station along EDSA, such as Ayala in Makati or Cubao, you can ride to
Ortigas Station
. The station is on the Ortigas Center side, and it is reportedly close enough to Robinsons Galleria to walk to the shrine.
Check the exact walking route and time on a map app. Fares depend on the distance, so confirm at the station ticket counter.
Trains are very crowded at rush hour, so keep your belongings secure.
Operating hours and fares can change, so check the latest announcements.

items.title: From the airport by taxi or Grab

children.text: If you go by car from Ninoy Aquino International Airport, the time varies greatly with traffic, so check the estimate in the Grab app.
Set the destination as "EDSA Shrine" or "Robinsons Galleria." The shrine has entrances on both the EDSA and Ortigas sides, so tell the driver where to drop you off.
City buses and the EDSA Carousel run past this area along EDSA. Stop locations and routes change often, so confirm locally.
The Robinsons Galleria side is known as a place to board buses, jeepneys and taxis.
The shrine, Robinsons Galleria and Ortigas Center are within walking distance of one another. To avoid sun and rain, use the passages inside the mall.
There have been periods when cars were not allowed inside the shrine grounds, so if you come by taxi, it is best to get off in front of the entrance.

The shrine has an open-air plaza and an underground church, so the weather affects it little. The plaza has little shade, though, so it is more comfortable to go in the morning or around sunset to avoid the midday heat.

Crowds of worshippers come around the revolution anniversary on February 25, during Holy Week (the week before Easter), and during the December dawn Masses (Simbang Gabi). A weekday morning is better if you want quiet, and a Sunday morning is good if you want to see a Sunday Mass.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Anniversary events around February 25 and Christmas-season events draw crowds.
The plaza gets hot, so go early in the morning or in the evening, and check the Holy Week schedule.
Good for shifting plans to the underground church and nearby malls, but EDSA traffic is heavy.

The shrine itself has no lodging or restaurants. Nor is it set up for eating or lingering inside, so it is easiest to eat outside before or after your visit. Robinsons Galleria next door has food courts, restaurants and cafes that are good for a meal around your visit. If you are not yet used to Filipino food, Korean and Japanese outlets are also easy to find inside the mall.

Hotels cluster around Ortigas Center and are popular with business travelers and tourists. Check location and rates against current information before booking; a place close to the shrine makes an early-morning visit easier. Plan a day that combines shopping at
Ortigas Center
and
Greenhills Shopping Center
Because this is a place of worship, we recommend modest clothing that covers the shoulders and knees. Avoid shorts and sleeveless tops.
During Mass, do not talk loudly or use a flash. Follow on-site signs on whether photos are allowed inside the church.
Sunday Masses are listed several times from morning to evening. Check the latest times on the shrine's official website or Facebook page.
The shrine has entrances on the EDSA side and the Ortigas Avenue side, and restrooms on both sides are reported (per the official September 2025 notice, so this may change).
The plaza has little shade, so bring a hat and water, and step into Robinsons Galleria to rest during the day.
EDSA is extremely congested at rush hour. Taking the train makes travel time easier to predict.
Rallies or events bring security checks and may restrict vehicles. On those days, change your plans or go early.
Reading about the revolution beforehand makes the reliefs and monuments much easier to appreciate. A visit together with the People Power Monument in Quezon City also works well.
On days with rallies or large events the area around the shrine can be closed off and vehicle access blocked, so check announcements in advance.
Because this is a place of worship, do not photograph people at prayer or make loud noise.
Watch for pickpockets and phone snatchers on the crowded EDSA sidewalks and footbridges.
Mass and office hours change often. Confirm the latest by checking the official website and calling.
It is also a place where political rallies are held, so at demonstrations it is safer not to stay long inside the crowd.
In the rainy season EDSA can flood or back up, so allow plenty of travel time.
This financial and commercial district has the shrine at its northern end, with shopping and dining areas you can explore on foot.
A large mall inside Ortigas Center along EDSA. Decide whether to walk or take a taxi from the shrine depending on the weather and your bags.
A shopping area on the San Juan side, about
10–30 minutes
away depending on traffic. It is known as a place packed with a wide variety of shops.
Quezon City's best-known city park; travel time varies greatly with traffic. It suits a day that includes a stroll.
